originalRequest: Author a complete English course for the open Agent-courses site at slug learn-agent-readable-repo, for a developer whose team or personal projects now have several people and several agent tools working in the same repository. Terminal task: write an AGENTS.md for one real repository and verify that agent behaviour changed in an observable way. Six lessons on what belongs in a repo-level instruction file and what does not, why one giant instruction file fails, nesting and nearest-wins resolution, writing commands rather than adjectives, instruction conflicts and priority ordering, and verifying that the file actually changed behaviour. Lesson 1 must draw the line between a repo instruction file and a Skill and then stay out of Skill territory, which belongs to learn-agent-skills-reuse. The course must not become a harness-construction tutorial; the organising thread is the open standard plus verifiable behaviour change. Verification here means 'did the instruction file change what the agent did', not 'is the code correct', which belongs to learn-verify-agent-output. The governance statement and the adoption number must be verified from primary sources during the session rather than repeated from memory or from a blog, and the AAIF 'Measuring AGENTS.md' five-run benchmark must be read before being cited.
learnerBrief: The reader owns or commits to a repository that several people and at least two different agent tools now work in. They can run the project's build and test commands and have run a coding agent on a task in it. Their problem is repetition: the same corrections — the package manager, the real test command, the generated directory nobody should hand-edit — get typed into every session, by every person, on every tool, because the repository never records them anywhere an agent reads. They are not building an agent or a harness; they want the repository itself to carry the context, and they want evidence that writing it down changed something rather than an assumption that it did.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The request supplied the target reader ('a developer whose team or personal projects now have several people and several agent tools working in the same repo'), the terminal task ('write an AGENTS.md for one real repository and verify that agent behaviour changed in an observable way'), the lesson count and all six themes verbatim, the concept ceiling (~7 per lesson), and three explicit scope boundaries against sibling courses: Skills belong to learn-agent-skills-reuse and Lesson 1 must draw that line and then stay out, verification gates belong to learn-verify-agent-output so verification here means behaviour change rather than code correctness, and the course must not become a harness-construction tutorial. It also specified source-verification requirements: confirm governance and the adoption figure from primary sources rather than memory or a blog, and read the AAIF benchmark before citing it. Starting point, goal, and constraints were all supplied; no clarification was needed.

learnerModel.targetReader: A developer who commits to a repository worked on by several people and at least two different coding-agent tools, and who keeps re-typing the same repo-specific corrections into every session.
knownConcepts: Running a coding agent on a task in a repository they own
Running the project's build, test, and lint commands from a terminal
Editing files, committing, and working on a branch
Reading a git diff and a directory tree
That agents sometimes do the wrong thing and need correcting
unknownConcepts: Any specific tool's configuration file format, flags, or discovery internals
How to build or modify an agent harness
Agent Skills authoring, which is a sibling course's subject
Hooks, permission systems, or sandboxed execution beyond knowing they exist as the enforcement layer
Statistical methods for experiment design beyond counting outcomes across repeated runs
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: Their own repository, terminal, editor, and at least one agent tool they can start fresh sessions in. The course assumes no per-run token accounting, no CI access, no second machine, and no embedded sandbox; every exercise runs against a repository the reader already has.
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: Run one `ls` at the repository root to find which instruction files already exist, and mark each existing line as non-obvious or discoverable — achievable with only a terminal and the reading from Lesson 1.
noviceRamp: Opens from the reader's own experience — a correction typed four times — rather than from the format, so the file is motivated before it is named; the term AGENTS.md arrives after the problem it solves.
Lesson 1's first action is a single `ls` against a repository they already have, requiring no new tool, no new filename, and nothing from the unknownConcepts list.
Every command in the course states where to run it, what success looks like, and treats an empty result as a valid finding rather than a failure — so no exercise turns into a hidden environment exam.

Tool-specific mechanics (Lesson 3) arrive only after the shared, vendor-neutral rule is established, and every vendor detail is stamped as a dated snapshot so the reader learns the mechanism rather than a click-path.

The measurement design in Lesson 6 is scaled to counting bad runs out of three rather than to statistics, and states its own limits explicitly so the reader is taught the size of claim their evidence supports.

scope: Covers the open AGENTS.md format and the judgment behind an instruction file's contents: the boundary against a README and against a portable Skill; the two costs of length (context on every session, adherence at the margins) plus one tool's hard size cap; nesting, nearest-file resolution as positional precedence, and how to compute placement from a rule's common ancestor; converting evaluative adjectives into lines carrying a trigger, an object, and an observable result; finding and resolving contradictions across an assembled instruction chain; and designing a repeated before/after comparison that separates a behaviour change from run-to-run variation. Deliberately excludes: authoring Agent Skills (learn-agent-skills-reuse), verification that code is correct or gates that block completion (learn-verify-agent-output), building or configuring an agent harness, prompt engineering for individual tasks, and any product's UI click-path. Tool-specific loading mechanics are taught as dated snapshots of the mechanism rather than as durable configuration reference.

topicCurrency.staleRisk: Highest risk: the tool support matrix and every per-vendor mechanic in Lessons 3 and 6 — filenames (whether Claude Code still requires bridging), discovery and walk depth, AGENTS.override.md, project_doc_max_bytes and its 32 KiB default, Amp's globs frontmatter and agents-md list, Copilot's .github/instructions path-scoped files, and the instruction-listing commands the Lesson 6 exercises depend on. All are stamped 'as of 2026-08-23' in the text. Second: the adoption figure, which is self-reported, undated on the site, and will drift; the course treats it as a claim about spread rather than effect, which limits the damage if it changes. Third: the AAIF benchmark is a single-author, single-repo study on a tool version that will move — the course cites its method as transferable and its numbers as bounded. Fourth: IFScale evaluated mid-2025 models and Control Illusion 2025-generation models on system/user conflicts; both are cited for mechanism with the setting stated, so newer models changing the numbers does not invalidate the lessons, but a re-check should confirm no newer work contradicts the shape.
topicCurrency.verificationNotes: The '60,000+' figure and the governance sentence were both re-fetched from agents.md this session rather than carried from the design brief, and governance was cross-checked against aaif.io/projects. A GitHub code-search count was attempted as an independent adoption measure and rejected: filename:AGENTS.md returns 811,008 files and path:AGENTS.md returns 142, neither of which is a repository count, so no independently measured adoption number is cited anywhere in the course. The site's '88 AGENTS.md files in the main OpenAI repo' example was checked against the openai/codex tree via the GitHub API, which returned 2 — the site says 'at time of writing' and does not name the repository precisely, so the course cites it as a dated illustration of the nesting pattern and states that the count moves, rather than repeating it as current.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: Three mermaid diagrams, one each in Lessons 2, 3, and 5, and none elsewhere. Lesson 2's shows the three measured degradation shapes branching from rising instruction count and converging on 'same file, different tool, different curve' — a table would have listed the three names without showing that they are different signatures rather than three severities of one problem, which is the judgment the lesson needs. Lesson 3's is the nesting and nearest-wins resolution diagram: it draws a repository tree, then uses dotted edges to show which files load for one specific edit and which stay out of context, because the load-bearing idea is that the file set is chosen by where work happens rather than by what exists — prose describing this reads as a rule and the diagram shows it as a selection. Lesson 5's shows the four inputs assembled into one context (personal global file, root file, nested file, chat prompt) converging on a single behaviour with no note saying which rule lost; the point is that the repository supplies only two of the four, which is spatial information. Lessons 1, 4, and 6 have none: Lesson 1's content is a two-column boundary that a table carries better, Lesson 4's is a sentence-level rewriting procedure with no structure to draw, and Lesson 6's comparison design is a numbered sequence whose worked example is already a results table.
weakestPoints: The outline came pre-set from the design brief — six lessons and their six themes were specified in the request — and this run was non-interactive, so no human confirmed the outline between Stage 3 and Stage 4. The prerequisite DAG is linear (01→02→03→04→05→06) and each lesson's opening assumes the previous one's artifact, which is coherent but was never tested against a reader. The riskiest untested assumption is that Lesson 2 (length and adherence) belongs before Lesson 3 (placement) rather than after; the argument for the current order is that nesting is presented as the fix for a cost the reader has just been shown, but a reader who already nests would find Lesson 2 a detour.

Every quantitative claim in the course comes from a setting other than the one the reader is in, and the course leans on three of them. IFScale measured keyword inclusion in a business report, not repository instructions. Control Illusion measured formatting conflicts across system and user messages, not files at different directory depths. The AAIF benchmark is the closest match and is one author, one repository, one agent, two tasks, published by the foundation that stewards the format. Each is stamped with its setting in the prose and in sources.md, and no percentage is presented as an expectation — but a reader skimming for numbers can still carry '27%' or '9.6–45.8%' away without the boundary attached, and the course cannot prevent that.

Lesson 6's comparison design (three runs per condition, alternating, count the bad runs) is my scaled-down adaptation of a five-run method and is declared as such, but it is underpowered by construction. A reader whose specific mistake occurs one run in four will most likely see zero occurrences in three baseline runs and conclude the rule is redundant. The lesson names this failure mode in the faded-example answer and tells the reader to check task ambiguity before deleting the rule, which is mitigation rather than a fix — the honest position is that the design detects frequent failures and is blind to occasional ones.

The three-part decomposition of a usable instruction line (trigger, object, observable result) in Lesson 4 is a synthesis of vendor examples, not a framework any source publishes, and the lesson says so in the text where it is introduced. It is useful and it is not validated: nothing establishes that lines carrying all three outperform lines carrying two, and the 'missing two of three signals an adjective' heuristic is a judgment call presented as a rule of thumb.

Vendor mechanics are the course's largest stale surface and they are load-bearing in two lessons rather than decorative. Lesson 3's three divergences and Lesson 6's instruction-listing commands are dated 2026-08-23 in the prose, but if a tool renames a command or changes its discovery order, Lesson 6's Level 1 exercise stops working as written and the reader has no in-course path to the new command beyond the fallback suggestion of asking the tool directly.
followUpChecks: Re-fetch all four vendor docs (Codex agents-md guide, Claude Code memory, Amp manual, Cursor rules) and confirm the instruction-listing commands in Lesson 6's Level 1 exercise still exist and still produce the described output; that exercise is the one most likely to break silently on a tool update.

Re-check the agents.md adoption figure and governance sentence, and re-attempt an independently measurable adoption proxy. The current course cites no measured count because none was obtainable this session; if a credible one appears, Lesson 1's treatment of the self-reported figure should be revised to cite both.

Search for newer controlled measurements of instruction-file effect, particularly any replication of the AAIF benchmark at more than one contributor's scale — the author explicitly invited this. A second independent data point would let Lesson 6 stop relying on the steward's own evidence for its central method.

Check whether newer instruction-hierarchy work (the IH-Benchmark and many-tier lines of research visible in 2026) supersedes Control Illusion's numbers or, more usefully, measures conflicts between instruction files rather than between system and user messages. That would let Lesson 5 cite evidence from its actual setting rather than by mechanism transfer.

Test Lesson 3's hotspot interaction and Lesson 6's predict block in the rendered reader, and re-read every lesson on the rendered page for the $ / remark-math trap, which the guard cannot catch and which was the worst defect in a previous pipeline dogfood.

acceptanceReview.terminalTask: Lesson 6's Level 2 exercise: the reader assembles an instruction file for a repository they own from Lessons 1-5 (scoped by the portability test, placed by common ancestor, every line carrying a trigger and an object and an observable result, the assembled chain audited for four conflict patterns), confirms every team tool loads it from both root and subdirectory, runs six alternating runs — three per condition — on the rule whose violation costs most, commits the file with a message stating what was tested and found, and writes a four-sentence report naming at least two things the evidence does not establish. The completion criteria require the commit to exist, the six runs to be recorded as counts rather than an average, and no credential to appear in the committed file.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Five body interaction blocks, one each in Lessons 1-5, none in Lesson 6, and one agentmentor-action in each of Lessons 1, 3, and 5. Lesson 1 uses agentmentor-check on the repo-file-versus-Skill boundary, because the tempting wrong answer (a real, important, team-specific release procedure belongs in the instruction file) is exactly the misconception the portability test exists to catch, and each distractor encodes a distinct wrong reason — importance, human-readability, and redundancy-as-safety. Lesson 2 uses agentmentor-order on the sequence of shortening moves, because the failure is procedural rather than factual: people split before deleting, which multiplies junk across files, and ordering is the only block type that checks a sequence. Lesson 3 uses agentmentor-hotspot on a four-node directory tree to place a coupling rule, which is the correct use of that type — a single-point judgment on a structure diagram where the wrong nodes are wrong for three distinguishable reasons, and where the most tempting node (the directory the rule is about) is the subject-matter trap. Lesson 4 uses agentmentor-fix on a real adjective-shaped migration rule, with three local deterministic checks (names a command in backticks, carries a trigger word, drops the word 'careful') that check the rewrite mechanically without pretending to execute anything. Lesson 5 uses agentmentor-check on conflict resolution, placed there because emphasis is the near-universal instinct and the only option with published evidence against it. Lesson 6 uses agentmentor-predict on a single-run comparison whose expected answer is 'nothing', because the reader must feel the pull of clean numbers before being told the method — this is the one block where predicting first genuinely changes what the reader takes from the following paragraphs. No lesson carries more than one body block. The three action cards are deliberately spaced and each targets a different failure: Lesson 1's makes the reader defend a keep against a specific test, Lesson 3's has the agent predict the loaded chain for a concrete path, and Lesson 5's hunts the implication conflict, which is the one class grep cannot find.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: Written for a developer who commits to a shared repository, runs an agent in it, and can run its build and test commands — not for someone building agent infrastructure and not for a non-programmer. Four hidden prerequisites were removed. First, no tool-specific configuration knowledge is assumed anywhere: every vendor mechanic appears as a dated snapshot illustrating a shared mechanism, and where the reader needs a command, the course gives the command, the expected output, and a fallback (ask the tool which files it loaded) for when the command has changed. Second, Skills are named and bounded in Lesson 1 and then never required — a reader who has not taken the Skills course loses nothing, because every Skill reference is 'this belongs elsewhere' rather than 'do this'. Third, no per-run token accounting, CI access, or statistical training is assumed in Lesson 6; the design counts bad runs out of three using git diff --stat and direct observation, and the analysis instruction is to compare counts rather than compute anything. Fourth, no existing instruction file is assumed: every exercise treats an empty result as a valid finding, and Lesson 1's Level 1 explicitly says so. The first independent action — running ls at the repository root and marking each line found as non-obvious or discoverable — needs only a terminal and Lesson 1's three tests, and it works identically whether the result is a list of files or nothing at all.
promotionNotes: Before any examples/ promotion, re-fetch the four vendor docs and confirm Lesson 6's instruction-listing commands still work as written — that exercise has the shortest shelf life in the course.

The course cites the AAIF benchmark, published by the format's own steward, as its central evidence for measurable behaviour change. The method is sound and the negative first result is reported rather than buried, and sources.md states the conflict of interest — but a second, independent measurement would materially strengthen Lesson 6 and should be sought at the next revision.

No independently measured adoption count exists in the course, by decision: the GitHub code-search proxies checked this session (811,008 files under filename:AGENTS.md, 142 under path:AGENTS.md) measure files rather than repositories and would have been misleading. If a credible measured count appears, revise Lesson 1's treatment of the self-reported figure rather than leaving the current framing in place.
Lesson 3's hotspot block and Lesson 6's predict block have not been checked in the rendered reader; do that plus a full $ / remark-math read-through of all six lessons before promotion.

nextSteps: Read Lesson 1 and run its Level 1 exercise against a repository you actually commit to — the ls takes thirty seconds and its result determines whether the rest of the course is about writing a file or fixing one.
Do Lesson 6's Level 1 load check early, out of order if you like: knowing which tools read which files changes how you place every rule in Lessons 3 and 5.
Bring the assembled chain from Lesson 5's audit back to an agent and ask it to find the contradiction by implication — that class survives your own review because you wrote both halves.

After the terminal task, feed the four-sentence report back to an agent and ask it to argue your claim is larger than your evidence supports; over-claiming is the standard failure at this sample size.
